result:
The other morning, I watched a spider rebuild its web between two fence posts in my backyard. It had been destroyed the night before by wind or maybe a bird, and now the spider was methodically spinning new silk, moving between anchor points with the patience of someone who knows the work must be done regardless of mood or weather.

What struck me was how unbothered it seemed. No lamenting the lost web, no standing still in frustration, just immediate, focused effort toward the next version. There was something almost meditative about watching it trace those geometric patterns, each strand placed with intention.

I think about how often I, by contrast, waste energy mourning what got torn down instead of rebuilding. The metaphor feels obvious, maybe too obvious, but sitting there with my coffee watching that small creature work, it landed differently than when I read similar sentiments in self-help books.

The web isn't permanent. It'll be destroyed again, probably sooner than I'd like. But each time, the spider starts over with the same steady attention. There's a kind of freedom in accepting that nothing we build lasts forever, and the real skill lies in our willingness to begin again.

I finished my coffee and went inside to start my day, thinking about all the small repairs I keep postponing, both literal and otherwise. Some of them are easier to tackle than others. But at minimum, I can try to approach them with even a fraction of that spider's quiet persistence.
